title: Thomas Aquinas: The Bellowing Ox
speaker: Mr. Isaiah Couch
series: Reformation Series: Minds of the Medieval Ages

outline.title: The Purpose of Studying Church History
subpoints: Reformation as a return to biblical truth, not a new invention
Meditation on God's servants is part of covenant faithfulness
The goal is worship, not mere knowledge

outline.title: Reassessing the Middle Ages
subpoints: Dispelling the myth of the 'Dark Ages' as a historical black hole
Acknowledging the sins and inconsistencies of the medieval church
Recognizing the faithful testimony of God's people during this era

outline.title: The Life and Context of Thomas Aquinas
subpoints: Born into nobility near Aquino, Italy, around 1224-1225
Early education at Monte Cassino Benedictine Abbey
Exposure to Aristotle and dialectical methods at the University of Naples

outline.title: The Theological Significance of 'What is God?'
subpoints: Aquinas' devotion to questions 3-26 of the Summa Theologica
The importance of deep inquiry and intellectual discipline
Moving from spiritual milk to solid food in faith

summary:
This sermon concludes the Reformation Series on the minds of the medieval ages by examining the life and theology of Thomas Aquinas. The speaker emphasizes that studying church history is not merely an academic exercise but a duty of covenant faithfulness, reminding believers that the Protestant Reformation was a return to biblical truth rather than the invention of a new faith. By meditating on the lives of medieval theologians, the church honors the God who kept His people faithful through centuries of challenge and change.

The presentation challenges the common perception of the Middle Ages as a 'dark' or empty period in history. While acknowledging the sins and inconsistencies of the medieval church, the speaker highlights the glorious testimony of God's promise to build His church. Figures like Aquinas are presented not as objects of boast, but as instruments through which God blessed the church with deeper theological understanding and intellectual rigor.

The sermon traces Aquinas' early life, from his noble birth in Italy to his formative years at the Benedictine Abbey of Monte Cassino and later at the University of Naples. It highlights his early obsession with the question 'What is God?' and his subsequent engagement with Aristotelian philosophy and dialectical methods. The speaker encourages the congregation to emulate this intellectual discipline, urging believers to seek a deeper, more mature understanding of God's will and to move beyond spiritual infancy toward solid food in their faith.

And we pray all this by the power of your spirit, through the work of your son, to your praise alone. Amen.
